paras: The killing of Kiah Baker was the fatal shooting of an elderly Black man on a road about three miles northeast of Hopkinsville, Christian County, Kentucky, in mid-April 1881. Before he died, Baker said one of three passing horsemen had shot him, while a rival story held that he was shot robbing a hen roost. A young man, Jas. B. Cannon, was arrested after boasting that he had done it, but was acquitted, and the local paper later recorded the killing as an assassination by "unknown parties."
Baker lived with F. S. Meacham three miles northeast of Hopkinsville. Wire reports described him as "an old colored man," and the local South Kentuckian called him "a negro man."

Baker had been away from home and returned about nine o'clock at night with a gunshot wound. He said he was walking along the road when three men on horseback came up behind him from the direction of the city and yelled at him to "clear the track." He stepped aside into a fence corner, and as the riders passed, one of them turned in his saddle and shot him through the body. Baker died the following day, having repeated, according to a Hopkinsville dispatch, the story of the three horsemen "just before dying."

The date is uncertain. The wire dispatch filed on April 18 placed the shooting on "last Friday night," the South Kentuckian on "Sunday night 18th inst.," and a later local report on "the night of the 9th." The paper's year-end chronology listed the killing under April 18, "on the Greenville road."

Within the following week, Jas. B. Cannon, a man of about 25, was heard at a log rolling, while drinking, to say that he "shot that nigger Saturday night." Several listeners reported him, and Deputy Sheriff Boyd arrested him and lodged him in jail. At his trial on April 25, prosecuted by County Attorney Brasher and defended by Col. L. A. Sypert, Cannon said he had spoken in jest and offered an alibi, and he was acquitted. No report of an inquest or of any further arrest appears in the coverage.

The South Kentuckian treated the case as a homicide, heading its first report "Another Homicide," printing Baker's account at length, and judging the hen-roost story "not substantiated." It predicted that "the manner of his shooting will remain a mystery," and in its review of 1881 it listed Baker as "assassinated by unknown parties."

Beyond Kentucky, a two-sentence dispatch from Hopkinsville ran in crime roundups from Memphis to Canton, Ohio, giving the horsemen and the hen-roost versions side by side. Rewritten briefs in Minnesota and Wisconsin papers a week later called him "Miah Baker" and dated the shooting to the 15th, and the Wheeling Register printed "Kirk Baker." Some editors made the rumor a joke: the Wheeling Register headlined the item "Probably After The Hen-Boost," and the Delaware State Journal wrote that "the horror of the story is mitigated" by the hint that Baker was too familiar with his slayer's hen roost.

Baker's own statement, as reported locally and by wire, was that a passing horseman shot him without cause beyond an order to clear the road. The competing claim, attributed only to unnamed "others," was that he was shot while robbing a hen roost, and the local paper noted that no one witnessed the shooting.

reader.title: Killing of Kiah Baker
bases: Baker said three men on horseback rode up behind him on the road and one of them shot him, a killing by a small group of private men with no stated official role (A2, A4); a rival report that he was shot robbing a hen roost leaves the shooter's identity and motive in doubt (A2, A5).

The local Hopkinsville paper (A2, A7, A10) and an independent Hopkinsville wire dispatch (A1, A4, A5) agree that Baker was shot and killed near Hopkinsville and both give his account of the three horsemen; they differ on the date and on how he came to be shot.

accounts.gist: Walking home along the road, he was overtaken by three horsemen from the direction of the city who yelled at him to 'clear the track'; he stepped into a fence corner and one rider turned in his saddle and shot him.

accounts.label: Hen-roost rumor
accounts.gist: Others said he was shot while robbing a hen roost; the local paper said this was not substantiated and that no one witnessed the shooting.

accounts.label: Cannon's reported boast
accounts.gist: Several people heard Jas. B. Cannon say at a log rolling that he had shot Baker on Saturday night; Cannon said he spoke in jest and was acquitted.

Most distant papers ran the two-sentence wire item in crime roundups such as 'Killings and Lynchings' without comment.

versions.value: Friday night (Apr 15), per the Apr 18 wire
Sunday night 18th inst., died the next day

conflicts.note: The wire was filed on Apr 18 and already reported Baker dead, so the shooting preceded that date; the local paper's 'Sunday night 18th' is internally inconsistent (Apr 18, 1881 was a Monday) and may mean Sunday the 17th, with death on the 18th, the date the year-end list uses. The Cannon article's '9th' and 'Saturday night' fit neither.
The local paper consistently prints 'Kiah'; the variants are wire and rewrite errors.

versions.value: Shot by one of three passing horsemen (Baker's statement)
Shot while robbing a hen roost (rumor)

conflicts.note: The local paper said the hen-roost story was not substantiated and there were no witnesses; Baker's own statement is the only first-hand account reported.

record_check.dossier: Kiah Baker in the local paper and most wires; 'Miah' and 'Kirk' are variants

Shooting date conflicts: Friday Apr 15 (wire), 'Sunday night 18th' with death next day (local), 'the 9th' (arrest report); Apr 18 is the wire filing date and the year-end listing date, and may be the date of death
Unknown per Baker's account (three horsemen); Jas. B. Cannon was arrested on his own reported boast and acquitted
Three horsemen by Baker's account; the rival hen-roost story implies a single property owner; no mob is described
At least 10 articles in 8 papers, first 1881-04-18, including three in the local South Kentuckian

info: Shot 'last Friday night' according to the Apr 18 wire dispatch
On the road about three miles northeast of Hopkinsville, near the home of F. S. Meacham, with whom Baker lived; the year-end list places it 'on the Greenville road'
Kiah Baker, described as an 'old colored man' (wire) and 'a negro man' (local paper); also printed as 'Kirk Baker' and 'Miah Baker'
No formal accusation; a rumor reported that he was shot while robbing a hen roost, which the local paper called 'not substantiated'
Per Baker: one of three men on horseback who came from the direction of the city; reported as 'unknown' by the local paper and the wire
Cannon acquitted; the year-end chronology still attributes the killing to 'unknown parties'
